title: Establishing Propagation Protocols for Buddleja saligna and Euclea natalensis
content: Buddleja saligna and Euclea natalensis are widely used in traditional medicine and have ornamental and cosmeceutical value. However, propagation methods are scarce, highlighting the need for sustainable propagation techniques to support commercialization and ensure a consistent supply of high-quality material. Therefore, this study investigated the influence of temperature on seed germination and seedling emergence, as well as the effects of cutting position, growth medium, season, and the use of a plant growth regulator on the success of vegetative propagation. Seed germination of B. saligna was highest at 25 °C (96%), with optimal mean germination time (3.1 days), mean emergence time (3.9 days), germination index (145.2), shortest time to 50% germination (2.6 days), and shortest time to 50% emergence (3.98 days). However, results were not significantly different from 20 °C and 30 °C. For E. natalensis, maximum germination (98%) occurred at 20 °C, with no significant differences to 25 °C and 30 °C. For B. saligna, significant interactions between season and cutting position affected leaf and bud formation. The best rooting percentage (7%) was achieved by stem cuttings treated with DynarootTM 3 (0.8% IBA) and planted in coco peat (M2). For E. natalensis, no survival or rooting was observed in any of the treatment combinations. Overall, seed propagation was more effective, but vegetative propagation is preferable for producing uniform high-quality extracts as seed propagation may introduce variation. Therefore, further research is needed to establish reliable vegetative propagation protocols for both species.
